text.q: Take care not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

verse.note: Here the word means doing what is right in practice. It heads the three examples that follow: giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so the same word can elsewhere be rendered 'justice'.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 9, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses often for God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it and the singular where the Greek is singular, as in verses 10 and 20.

text.q: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that people will praise them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

verse.note: The Greek word originally meant a stage actor, but in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it already meant a godless or insincere person, and elsewhere this translation renders it 'hypocrites'. In this chapter the passage is about religion staged for an audience, with trumpets, street corners and being seen. The theatrical sense is therefore live, and 'performers' is used in verses 2, 5 and 16.

note.term: they have been paid their reward in full

verse.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period for acknowledging payment in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone. The account is settled and nothing further is owed. Many modern translations similarly render 'they have received their reward in full'.

verse.text: ⟦Now having risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.

note.term: Now having risen early on the first day of the week

verse.note: The double brackets around verses 9–20 mark the longer ending. It appears in the great majority of manuscripts and was known by the late second century, but it is absent from the two earliest, joins awkwardly to verse 8, and differs from Mark in style and vocabulary. Nearly all scholars regard it as an early addition that draws on the resurrection accounts in the other Gospels and Acts; many churches nonetheless receive it as Scripture.
